o1_1.html:
The exam describes a control and asks you to classify it. Ask two questions:

  1. Category — HOW is it implemented? By technology, by management policy, by people doing a process, or physically.
  2. Type — WHAT does it do? Stop it, discourage it, notice it, fix it, stand in for something, or tell people what to do.

One control has one category and one primary type. A badge reader is Physical (category) and Preventive (type).

CategoryMeaningExamples
Technical (logical)Implemented by systemsFirewall, encryption, MFA, antivirus, ACLs
Managerial (administrative)Decisions and oversight: policies, riskRisk assessment, security policy, hiring standards
OperationalDay-to-day procedures carried out by peopleGuards patrolling, log review, backups, awareness training delivery
PhysicalTangible barriers in the real worldFences, locks, bollards, mantraps, lighting
TrapManagerial = deciding and documenting. Operational = people doing the task. "A guard checks badges" is operational; "a policy requires badges" is managerial.

TypeJobExample
PreventiveStops the event before it happensFirewall deny rule, door lock, least privilege
DeterrentDiscourages an attempt (doesn't physically stop it)Warning sign, visible camera, login banner
DetectiveIdentifies/records an event during or afterIDS, SIEM alerts, log review, motion sensor
CorrectiveLimits damage and restores after the eventRestore from backup, patch after exploit, quarantine
CompensatingAn alternative when the primary control can't be usedSegmenting a legacy system that can't be patched
DirectiveTells people what to do (relies on compliance)Policy, "authorized personnel only" sign, AUP

• Timing is the fastest clue: before → preventive/deterrent; during/after noticing → detective; after, fixing → corrective.
  • "Can't / unable / legacy / instead" → compensating.
  • Sign or banner: if it warns of consequences → deterrent; if it instructs → directive.
  • A camera that is monitored or recorded is detective; a visible camera meant to scare people off is deterrent. Read for intent.

o1_2.html:
• Confidentiality — only authorized people can read it (encryption, access control).
  • Integrity — it hasn't been altered (hashing, digital signatures, FIM).
  • Availability — it's there when needed (redundancy, backups, DDoS protection).
  • Non-repudiation — the sender can't deny sending it: digital signatures (private key) give proof of origin + integrity.

Authentication proves identity (password, MFA, certificate). Authorization decides what that identity may do (permissions, roles). Accounting records what it did (logs, audit trails). Authenticate people and systems (device certificates, 802.1X). Authorization models appear in 4.6.
Compare where you are (current state) with where you need to be (a framework or target state, e.g. NIST CSF or ISO 27001), then list the gaps and a plan to close them.

Never trust based on network location — verify every request (identity, device posture, context) and grant least privilege.

Control plane (decides)Data plane (enforces)
Policy Engine — makes the allow/deny decision
Policy Administrator — tells the enforcement point to open/close the session
Adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control		Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) — the gate traffic actually passes through
Subject/system → PEP → resource
Implicit trust zones — the area behind the PEP

Memory hook: judge (engine) decides, clerk (administrator) does the paperwork, bailiff (PEP) guards the door.

• Bollards (stop vehicles), access control vestibule (mantrap — stops tailgating), fencing, lighting, guards, access badges, video surveillance.
  • Sensors: infrared (heat/motion), pressure, microwave, ultrasonic.
  • Deception: honeypot (one fake system), honeynet (a network of them), honeyfile (bait file that alerts when opened), honeytoken (fake credential/record that alerts when used). They waste attacker time and generate high-fidelity alerts.

o1_3.html:
• Approval process — usually a Change Advisory Board (CAB) approves.
  • Ownership — a named owner is accountable for the change.
  • Stakeholders — everyone affected is identified and informed.
  • Impact analysis — what could break, what risk is introduced.
  • Test results — proof it works in a test/staging environment first.
  • Backout plan — how to roll back if it fails (rollback ≠ "hope").
  • Maintenance window — scheduled time with least business impact.
  • SOP — standard operating procedure for routine changes.

• Allow/deny lists may need updating for new software.
  • Restricted activities — change only what was approved (scope).
  • Downtime, service restart, application restart — plan and communicate.
  • Legacy applications may break; dependencies must be mapped.

After the change: update diagrams, update policies/procedures, and use version control for configs and code so you can see and revert exactly what changed.

Why security caresUnapproved or untested changes are a top cause of outages and new vulnerabilities. Change management keeps availability and integrity.

o1_4.html:
SymmetricAsymmetric
KeysOne shared secretPublic/private key pair
SpeedFast — bulk dataSlow — small data, key exchange, signatures
ExamplesAES, ChaCha20 (3DES/DES legacy)RSA, ECC, Diffie-Hellman (key exchange)

Real systems combine them: asymmetric to exchange a session key, symmetric to encrypt the data (that's TLS).

  • Encrypt for someone → their public key. Only their private key decrypts.
  • Sign → your private key. Anyone verifies with your public key → integrity + non-repudiation.

• Hash (SHA-256): one-way fingerprint; any change → different hash. Integrity, password storage. MD5/SHA-1 are broken (collisions).
  • Salt: random value added per password before hashing → defeats rainbow tables, identical passwords get different hashes.
  • Key stretching (PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2): many iterations → brute force is slower.
  • Digital signature = hash the message, encrypt the hash with the private key.

Levels: full-disk (BitLocker, FileVault), partition, volume, file, database, record (a single row/field). Transport encryption: TLS, IPsec, VPN. Key length matters (AES-256 vs 128); key exchange (Diffie-Hellman) lets two parties agree on a secret over an open channel.

ToolWhat it is
TPMChip on the motherboard: stores keys for one device, measured/secure boot, BitLocker
HSMDedicated appliance/card that generates and protects keys at scale (CAs, payment)
KMSKey management system (often cloud) — lifecycle and rotation
Secure enclaveIsolated processor area for secrets (phones)

• Steganography — hide data inside other data (an image).
  • Tokenization — replace sensitive data with a token; the mapping lives in a secure vault (card numbers).
  • Data masking — show only part (***-**-1234).

• CA signs certificates; trust flows root CA → intermediate → leaf. Self-signed = no third-party trust.
  • CSR (certificate signing request) is what you send a CA; it contains your public key.
  • Wildcard (*.example.com) covers subdomains; SAN lists multiple names.
  • Revocation: CRL (a published list) vs OCSP (real-time query); OCSP stapling — the server attaches the response.
  • Key escrow — a trusted third party holds a copy of keys for recovery.
  • Blockchain — distributed, append-only ledger; open public ledger.

o2_1.html:
ActorResources / sophisticationTypical motivation
Nation-stateHighest; APTs that persist for monthsEspionage, war/disruption of infrastructure, political
Unskilled attackerLow; uses others' tools/scriptsThrill, notoriety, disruption
HacktivistVariesPhilosophical/political beliefs — defacement, leaks, DDoS
Insider threatHas legitimate accessRevenge, financial gain, (or careless mistakes)
Organized crimeHigh; well fundedFinancial gain — ransomware, fraud, data theft
Shadow ITEmployees, no malicious intentConvenience — unapproved apps/cloud create risk

• Internal vs external — inside the organization or not.
  • Resources/funding — nation-state and organized crime are highest.
  • Level of sophistication/capability.

Data exfiltration · espionage · service disruption · blackmail · financial gain · philosophical/political beliefs · ethical (white-hat disclosure) · revenge · disruption/chaos · war.

TrapMotivation is why, not what happened. Encrypted files is the effect; financial gain (ransom) is the motivation. Insider vs Shadow IT turns on malicious intent.

o2_2.html:
• Message-based: email, SMS (smishing), instant messaging.
  • Image-based and file-based (malicious attachments, macros), voice call (vishing), removable device (USB drops).
  • Vulnerable software: client-based (agent installed) vs agentless; unsupported systems and applications (end-of-life, no patches).
  • Unsecure networks: wireless, wired, Bluetooth.
  • Open service ports, default credentials.
  • Supply chain: managed service providers (MSPs), vendors, suppliers.

TermClue
PhishingBroad email lure
Spear phishing / whalingTargeted / targets executives
Vishing / smishingVoice / SMS
Misinformation / disinformationFalse info (accidental / deliberate)
Impersonation, pretextingPretending to be someone with a made-up story
Business email compromise (BEC)Compromised/spoofed exec or vendor account asks for payment change
Watering holeCompromise a site the targets visit
Brand impersonationFake site/emails using a known brand
TyposquattingLook-alike domain: examp1e.com

o2_3.html:
• Memory injection, buffer overflow (writing past a buffer's end), race condition — including TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use).
  • Malicious update — a trusted update channel delivers malware.

• SQL injection — input changes the meaning of a database query. Fix: parameterized queries, input validation.
  • Cross-site scripting (XSS) — attacker-supplied script runs in other users' browsers. Fix: output encoding, CSP, input validation.

• OS-based flaws; firmware; end-of-life / legacy hardware.
  • Virtualization: VM escape (break out to the hypervisor), resource reuse (data left in reallocated memory/disk).
  • Cloud-specific: misconfigured storage, exposed keys.
  • Supply chain: service, hardware or software providers.
  • Cryptographic: weak algorithms, bad key handling.
  • Misconfiguration: open ports, default settings, permissive permissions.
  • Mobile: side loading (apps from outside the store), jailbreaking/rooting.
  • Zero-day: unknown to the vendor; no patch exists yet.

o2_4.html:
MalwareTell-tale sign
RansomwareFiles encrypted, ransom note
TrojanLooks legitimate, hides malicious function
WormSpreads by itself across the network
VirusNeeds a host file/user action to spread
Spyware / keyloggerWatches activity / records keystrokes
RootkitHides deep in the OS (kernel), evades tools
Logic bombTriggers on a date/event
BloatwareUnwanted preinstalled software

• DDoS (amplified/reflected — small request, big response sent to the victim), DNS attacks, on-path (man-in-the-middle), credential replay, wireless attacks.
  • Injection, buffer overflow, replay, privilege escalation, forgery (CSRF/SSRF), directory traversal (../../etc/passwd).
  • Physical: brute force (forcing a door), RFID cloning, environmental.
  • Crypto: downgrade (force weaker protocol), collision, birthday.

• Brute force: many passwords against one account → lockouts on one user.
  • Password spraying: one or a few common passwords against many accounts → a few failures per user across many users, avoiding lockout.
  • Dictionary, credential stuffing (reusing leaked username/password pairs).

Account lockout · concurrent session usage · blocked content · impossible travel (logins from two distant places minutes apart) · resource consumption · resource inaccessibility · out-of-cycle logging · published/documented (the data shows up online) · missing logs (attacker covering tracks).

o2_5.html:
• Segmentation — split the network so a breach can't spread (VLANs, subnets, microsegmentation).
  • Access control — ACLs and permissions.
  • Application allow list — only approved software runs (stronger than a deny list).
  • Isolation — quarantine a suspect host.
  • Patching, encryption, monitoring, least privilege.
  • Configuration enforcement — baselines pushed and checked (GPO, MDM, config management).
  • Decommissioning — retire systems properly (wipe, remove from inventory/DNS).

• Encryption, installing endpoint protection (EDR), host-based firewall, HIPS.
  • Disable ports/protocols and services you don't need.
  • Change default passwords.
  • Remove unnecessary software — smaller attack surface.

o3_1.html:
ModelYou manageProvider manages
IaaSOS, apps, data, configHardware, hypervisor, facility
PaaSApps, dataRuntime, OS, infrastructure
SaaSData, users, accessAlmost everything else

The responsibility matrix (shared responsibility model) defines who secures what. Hybrid = on-prem + cloud. Third-party vendors add supply-chain risk.

• Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — infrastructure defined in templates: repeatable, reviewable, but a bad template replicates mistakes everywhere.
  • Serverless — run functions without managing servers; provider handles the OS.
  • Microservices — small independent services talking over APIs; more API surface to secure.
  • Network infrastructure: physical isolation (air gap), logical segmentation, SDN (software-defined networking — control plane separated from data plane).
  • Centralized vs decentralized — single point of control/failure vs distributed resilience but harder governance.
  • Containerization (share the host kernel, lightweight) vs virtualization (full guest OS on a hypervisor).

• IoT — weak defaults, rarely patched → segment them.
  • ICS/SCADA — industrial control; availability and safety first, legacy protocols → isolate/air-gap.
  • RTOS — real-time OS with strict timing (vehicles, medical).
  • Embedded systems — fixed-function, hard to patch.
  • High availability — redundancy so a failure doesn't stop service.

Considerations the exam lists: availability, resilience, cost, responsiveness, scalability, ease of deployment, risk transference, ease of recovery, patch availability, inability to patch, power, compute.

o3_2.html:
• Security zones: internet (untrusted) → screened subnet/DMZ (public-facing servers) → internal → restricted. Place devices by what must reach them.
  • Fail-open keeps traffic flowing if the device fails (availability); fail-closed blocks everything (security).
  • Inline / active devices sit in the traffic path and can block (IPS); tap / monitor / passive devices see a copy and only alert (IDS).

DevicePurpose
Jump serverHardened host admins go through to reach secure zones
Proxy serverMakes requests on behalf of clients; filtering, caching (reverse proxy = in front of servers)
IDS / IPSDetect / detect + block (signature or anomaly)
Load balancerSpreads traffic across servers (active/active, active/passive)
SensorsCollect traffic/data for monitoring
WAFLayer-7 firewall for web apps (SQLi, XSS)
UTMAll-in-one: firewall, IPS, AV, filtering
NGFWApplication-aware firewall with IPS and identity
Layer 4 vs Layer 7 firewallPorts/IPs vs application content

• 802.1X port-based NAC with EAP, usually backed by RADIUS — authenticate before the port passes traffic.
  • VPN: remote access (user) or site-to-site. IPsec: AH = integrity/authentication only, ESP = encryption + integrity; tunnel mode encrypts the whole packet (site-to-site), transport mode just the payload. TLS VPN works through browsers.
  • SD-WAN — software-defined WAN across links (broadband, LTE, MPLS).
  • SASE — cloud-delivered networking + security (SD-WAN, SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) close to users.

o3_3.html:
• Types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual property, legal, financial, human- vs non-human-readable.
  • Classifications: sensitive, confidential, public, restricted, private, critical. Classification decides the controls.

StateProtect with
At rest (stored)Full-disk / database / file encryption, permissions
In transit (moving)TLS, IPsec, VPN
In use (in memory/processing)Secure enclaves, memory protection, access control

Data sovereignty — data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored. Geolocation — restrict where data/users can be.

• Encryption (reversible with the key) vs hashing (one-way).
  • Masking — hide part of the value for display (****1234).
  • Tokenization — substitute a meaningless token; original kept in a vault.
  • Obfuscation — make it hard to understand.
  • Segmentation — keep sensitive data in separate zones.
  • Permission restrictions — least privilege on the data itself.

o3_4.html:
• High availability: load balancing vs clustering (servers acting as one, failover).
  • Sites: hot (ready now, most expensive), warm (hardware, needs data/config), cold (space and power only, cheapest, slowest). Geographic dispersion so one disaster can't take both.
  • Platform diversity and multi-cloud avoid single-vendor failure.
  • Continuity of operations (COOP), capacity planning (people, technology, infrastructure).

MetricMeans
RPOMax acceptable data loss, in time (e.g. 4 h → back up at least every 4 h)
RTOMax time to restore service
MTTRMean time to repair
MTBFMean time between failures (reliability)

• Full — everything; fastest restore.
  • Incremental — changes since the last backup of any kind; fastest backup; restore = last full + every incremental since.
  • Differential — changes since the last full; restore = last full + the latest differential.
  • Snapshots, replication (near-real-time copy), journaling, onsite vs offsite, frequency, encryption of backups.
Testing: tabletop exercises (discussion), fail over, simulation, parallel processing. Power: UPS (short-term battery, clean shutdown), generators (long-term).

o4_1.html:
Establish (from vendor guides, CIS Benchmarks), deploy (GPO, MDM, configuration management, IaC) and maintain (scan for drift, update as threats change).

Hardening targets: mobile devices, workstations, switches, routers, cloud infrastructure, servers, ICS/SCADA, embedded systems, RTOS, IoT — disable what you don't need, change defaults, patch, restrict management access.

• WPA3 — SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces PSK handshake; resists offline dictionary attacks. WPA2 still common.
  • AAA/RADIUS for enterprise Wi-Fi with 802.1X/EAP (EAP-TLS uses certificates on both sides; PEAP uses a server certificate + password).
  • Site survey and heat maps to place access points and find rogue APs; installation considerations.

• MDM — enforce PIN, encryption, remote wipe, app control.
  • Deployment models: BYOD (user owns), COPE (corporate-owned, personally enabled), CYOD (choose from an approved list).
  • Connection methods: cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth.

• Input validation (server side), secure cookies (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite), static code analysis (SAST), code signing.
  • Sandboxing — run untrusted code in an isolated environment.
  • Monitoring of applications and systems.

o4_2.html:
• Acquisition/procurement — buy from approved vendors with security requirements.
  • Assignment/accounting — ownership (who is accountable) and classification.
  • Monitoring/asset tracking — inventory and enumeration (discovering what is actually on the network).

MethodWhat it does
SanitizationOverwrite/erase so data can't be recovered; device can be reused
DestructionShred, pulverize, incinerate, degauss (magnetic media) — device is gone
CertificationDocumented proof (certificate of destruction) from the vendor
Data retentionKeep data as long as required by law/policy — no longer
TrapDegaussing does nothing to SSDs (no magnetic storage) — use cryptographic erase or physical destruction.

o4_3.html:
• Vulnerability scan (credentialed = deeper, non-credentialed = attacker's view), application security: static analysis (code), dynamic analysis (running app), package monitoring.
  • Threat feeds: OSINT, proprietary, information-sharing organizations (ISACs), dark web.
  • Penetration testing, responsible disclosure / bug bounty, system/process audit.

• CVE = the ID of a specific vulnerability. CVSS = its severity score (0–10).
  • False positive = reported but not real; false negative = real but missed (the dangerous one).
  • Prioritize by severity and exposure, environmental variables, industry/organizational impact, and risk tolerance. An internet-facing CVSS 8 often beats an isolated CVSS 9.

• Response: patching, insurance, segmentation, compensating controls, exceptions and exemptions (documented, time-limited acceptance).
  • Validation: rescanning, audit, verification.
  • Reporting to stakeholders.

o4_4.html:
• Log aggregation — collect logs centrally.
  • Alerting and alert response/remediation/validation; quarantine.
  • Alert tuning — reduce false positives so real alerts get attention.
  • Scanning, reporting, archiving (retention for investigations/compliance).

ToolWhat it does
SIEMAggregates and correlates logs from many sources; alerts and dashboards
SCAPStandards for automated configuration/vulnerability checking
BenchmarksSecure configuration standards to check against
Agent vs agentlessSoftware on the host vs remote checks
AntivirusSignature/heuristic malware detection
DLPDetects/blocks sensitive data leaving
SNMP trapsDevices push alerts to a manager
NetFlowMetadata about traffic flows (who talked to whom, how much) — not content
Vulnerability scannersFind known weaknesses

o4_5.html:
• Firewall rules, access lists, ports/protocols, screened subnets.
  • IDS/IPS: trends and signatures.
  • Web filter: agent-based, centralized proxy, URL scanning, content categorization, block rules, reputation.
  • DNS filtering — block lookups of malicious domains.
  • NAC — check device posture before network access.

RecordPurpose
SPFDNS list of servers allowed to send for the domain
DKIMCryptographic signature on the message proving it wasn't altered and came from the domain
DMARCPolicy telling receivers what to do when SPF/DKIM fail (none/quarantine/reject) and where to send reports

Plus a gateway that filters spam/malware.

• OS security: Group Policy (Windows), SELinux (mandatory access control on Linux).
  • Secure protocols: choose the protocol, the port and the transport method (SSH not Telnet, SFTP not FTP, LDAPS not LDAP, HTTPS, SNMPv3).
  • File integrity monitoring (FIM) — alerts when critical files change.
  • DLP, EDR (endpoint detection & response) / XDR (extended across endpoints, network, cloud, email).
  • User behavior analytics (UBA) — baselines normal user activity and flags anomalies.

o4_6.html:
• Provisioning/de-provisioning, permission assignments, identity proofing (verify who someone really is), attestation (periodic review/recertification of access).
  • Federation — trust identities from another organization.
  • SSO: LDAP (directory queries), SAML (XML assertions, enterprise web SSO), OAuth (delegated authorization — "let this app access my calendar"), OpenID Connect (authentication layer on OAuth).

ModelDecided by
MAC (mandatory)Labels/clearances set by the system/admins (military)
DAC (discretionary)The owner of the resource
RBAC (role-based)Job role
Rule-basedSystem-wide rules (e.g. firewall ACLs)
ABAC (attribute-based)Attributes: user, resource, environment (dept=HR AND time=9–5)
Time-of-day restrictionsWhen access is allowed

Plus least privilege.

• Factors: something you know (password, PIN), have (token, phone, smart card), are (biometrics), somewhere you are (location). Two of the same factor is not MFA.
  • Implementations: biometrics, hard/soft authentication tokens, security keys (FIDO2).
  • Passwords: length, complexity, reuse, expiration, age; password managers; passwordless.
  • PAM: just-in-time permissions, password vaulting, ephemeral credentials.

o4_7.html: User provisioning · resource provisioning · guard rails · security groups · ticket creation · escalation · enabling/disabling services and access · continuous integration and testing · integrations and APIs. SOAR platforms run playbooks that automate response.

BenefitsConsiderations
Efficiency/time saving · enforcing baselines · standard infrastructure configurations · scaling securely · employee retention · reaction time · workforce multiplierComplexity · cost · single point of failure · technical debt · ongoing supportability

o4_8.html:
1. Preparation — plans, tools, training, contacts.
  2. Detection — notice something is wrong.
  3. Analysis — confirm and scope the incident.
  4. Containment — stop the spread (isolate hosts, block accounts).
  5. Eradication — remove the cause (malware, accounts, vulnerabilities).
  6. Recovery — restore systems and monitor.
  7. Lessons learned — what to improve.

Testing: tabletop exercise and simulation. Root cause analysis after. Threat hunting proactively searches for threats that evaded detection.

• Legal hold — preserve relevant data; don't delete.
  • Chain of custody — documented record of who handled evidence, when.
  • Acquisition (image the drive, capture memory), preservation (hashes prove integrity), reporting, e-discovery.
  • Order of volatility — collect the most volatile first: CPU registers/cache → RAM → swap/temp → disk → remote logs → archival/backup media.

o4_9.html:
SourceAnswers
Firewall logsWhich connections were allowed/blocked, from where
Application logsWhat the app did, errors, user actions
Endpoint logsProcess launches, EDR detections on hosts
OS-specific security logsLogons, privilege use, account changes
IDS/IPS logsWhich signatures fired
Network logsSwitch/router events, DHCP, DNS
MetadataEmail headers, file properties — who/when/where, not content
Vulnerability scans (was it exposed?), automated reports, dashboards (trend at a glance), packet captures (full content of traffic — the most detail, the most storage).

o5_1.html:
DocumentIs it mandatory?Example
PolicyYes — high-level intent from leadershipAUP, information security policy, BC/DR, IR, SDLC, change management policies
StandardYes — specific measurable requirementPassword, access control, physical security, encryption standards
ProcedureYes — step-by-step howChange management, onboarding/offboarding, playbooks
GuidelineNo — recommendation"Consider using a password manager"

• External: regulatory, legal, industry, local/regional, national, global.
  • Monitoring and revision — documents are reviewed on a schedule and after changes.
  • Structures: boards, committees, government entities; centralized vs decentralized governance.

RoleResponsibility
OwnerSenior person accountable for the data; decides classification
ControllerDecides why and how personal data is processed (privacy law)
ProcessorProcesses data on behalf of the controller (e.g. a payroll vendor)
Custodian / stewardDay-to-day handling: backups, permissions, data quality

o5_2.html:
• Assessments: ad hoc, recurring, one-time, continuous.
  • Qualitative — low/medium/high, heat maps, judgment. Quantitative — money and numbers.
TermFormula / meaning
AV asset valueWhat the asset is worth
EF exposure factor% of the asset lost in one event
SLEAV × EF — loss from one event
AROHow many times per year (0.2 = once every 5 years)
ALESLE × ARO — expected yearly loss

• Risk register: each risk with key risk indicators, risk owners and the risk threshold.
  • Risk tolerance — acceptable variation. Risk appetite: expansionary (seeks risk for growth), conservative (avoids), neutral.

StrategyWhat it means
TransferShift it to someone else — insurance, outsourcing
AcceptLive with it (exemption / exception documented)
AvoidStop the risky activity entirely
MitigateAdd controls to reduce likelihood or impact

Inherent risk (before controls) − controls = residual risk (what remains).
The BIA identifies critical functions and sets RTO (time to restore), RPO (acceptable data loss), and uses MTTR/MTBF for reliability.

o5_3.html:
• Vendor assessment: penetration testing, right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments, supply chain analysis.
  • Selection: due diligence, check for conflicts of interest.
  • Vendor monitoring, questionnaires, rules of engagement (what testers may and may not do).

AgreementPurpose
SLAMeasurable service levels: uptime, response time, penalties
MOAMemorandum of agreement — formal terms of cooperation
MOUMemorandum of understanding — intent to work together, usually not binding
MSAMaster service agreement — umbrella terms for future work
SOW / WOStatement of work / work order — specific tasks, deliverables, timeline under the MSA
NDANon-disclosure — keep information confidential
BPABusiness partners agreement — how partners share profit/loss and responsibilities

o5_4.html:
• Reporting: internal and external (to regulators).
  • Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts.
  • Monitoring: due diligence/care, attestation and acknowledgement, internal and external, automation.

• Legal implications: local/regional, national, global (e.g. GDPR in the EU).
  • Data subject — the person the data is about; rights include access and the right to be forgotten.
  • Controller vs processor (see 5.1), ownership, data inventory and retention.

PCI DSS (card data), HIPAA (US health), GDPR (EU personal data), SOX (financial reporting), GLBA (financial institutions), NIST CSF / RMF, ISO 27001 (ISMS) / 27002 (controls), CIS Controls, SOC 2 (service organization controls).

o5_5.html:
• Internal: compliance, audit committee, self-assessments.
  • External: regulatory, examinations, assessment, independent third-party audit.
  • Attestation — an auditor formally states controls meet requirements.

• Types: physical, offensive (red team), defensive (blue team), integrated (purple — red and blue together).
  • Knowledge of the environment: known (full info, white box), partially known (gray box), unknown (no info, black box).
  • Reconnaissance: passive (OSINT, no contact with targets) vs active (scanning that touches targets).
  • Always with written authorization and rules of engagement — scope, timing, what is off-limits.

o5_6.html:
• Phishing campaigns — simulated phishing, teach users to recognize and respond (report, don't click).
  • Anomalous behavior recognition: risky, unexpected or unintentional behavior.
  • User guidance/training: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider threat, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, hybrid/remote work environments.
  • Reporting and monitoring: initial and recurring; track metrics (click rate, report rate).
  • Development and execution — plan, deliver, measure, improve.
What success looks likeThe metric that matters most is the report rate: people who report a phish quickly turn every employee into a sensor.
